title: What Celsus leaves out about Joseph
source_text: Παραῤῥίπτει δ᾿ ὁ Κέλσος τὴν ἀπέχθειαν, οἶμαι τοῦ Ἠσαῦ πρὸς τὸν Ἰακὼβ, ἀνδρὸς κατὰ τὴν γραφὴν ὁμολογουμένου φαύλου· καὶ μὴ σαφῶς ἐκτιθέμενος τὰ περὶ τὸν Συμέων καὶ τὸν Λευῒ, ἐπεξελθόντας τῇ ὕβρει τῆς ἀδελφῆς βιασθείσης ὑπὸ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ βασιλέως Σικίμων, σφᾶς αἰτιᾶται· ἀδελφοὺς δὲ πωλοῦντας τοὺς υἱοὺς λέγει τοῦ Ἰακὼβ, καὶ ἀδελφὸν πιπρασκόμενον τὸν Ἰωσὴφ, καὶ πατέρα ἐξαπατώμενον τὸν Ἰακὼβ, ἐπεὶ μηδὲν ὑπονοήσας περὶ τῶν υἱῶν ἐπιδεικνύντων „τὸν ποικίλον χιτῶνα“ τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ ἀλλὰ πιστεύσας αὐτοῖς „ἐπένθει ὡς ἀπολωλότα τὸν Ἰωσὴφ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ δουλεύοντα, ὅρα δὲ τινα τρόπον ἀπεχθῶς καὶ οὐ φιλαλήθως συνήγαγε τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς ἱστοριας ὁ Κέλσος· ὥστε ὅπου μὲν ἐδόκει αὐτῷ κατηγορίαν περιέχειν ἡ ἱστορια, ἐκτιθεται αὐτὴν, ὅπου δὲ σωφροσύνης ἀξιολόγου ἐπίδειξις γεγένηται, τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ οὖκ ἐνδόντος πρὸς τὸν ἔρωτα τῆς νομιζομένης δεσποίνης πῆ μὲν παρακαλούσης πῇ δ᾿ ἀπειλούσης, οὐδ᾿ ὑπεμνήσθη τῆς ἱστορίας. πολλῶ γὰρ κρείττονα τῶν κατὰ τὸν Βελλεροφόντην ἱστορουμένων ἴδοιμεν ἂν τὸν Ἰωσὴφ, ἑλόμενον κατακλεισθῆναι ἐν φυλακῇ ἤπερ ἀπολέσαι νοῦν σώφρονα· δυνάμενος γοῦν ἀπολογίσασθαι καὶ δικαιολογήσασθαι πρὸς τὴν κατηγορήσασαν μεγαλοψύχως ἀπεσιώπησε τῷ θεῷ ἐπιτρέψας τὰ καθ᾿ ἑαυτόν.
pass_a_gloss: Celsus throws in alongside (παραρρίπτει) the hatred (ἀπέχθειαν), I think of Esau toward Jacob, a man according to the scripture acknowledged (ὁμολογουμένου) base/worthless (φαύλου); and not clearly setting out (ἐκτιθέμενος) the things about Simeon and Levi, who went after/avenged (ἐπεξελθόντας) the outrage (ὕβρει) of the sister forced (βιασθείσης) by the son of the king of the Shechemites, he blames them (σφᾶς αἰτιᾶται); and he speaks of brothers selling (πωλοῦντας), the sons of Jacob, and a brother being sold (πιπρασκόμενον), Joseph, and a father being deceived (ἐξαπατώμενον), Jacob, since suspecting (ὑπονοήσας) nothing about the sons showing 'the many-coloured tunic (ποικίλον χιτῶνα)' of Joseph but believing them he 'mourned (ἐπένθει)' as lost (ἀπολωλότα) Joseph serving as slave (δουλεύοντα) in Egypt. See in what way hatefully (ἀπεχθῶς) and not truth-lovingly (φιλαλήθως) Celsus gathered (συνήγαγε) the things from the history; so that where the history seemed to him to contain accusation (κατηγορίαν), he sets it out, but where a display (ἐπίδειξις) of notable chastity/self-control (σωφροσύνης) occurred, Joseph not giving in (ἐνδόντος) to the love/passion (ἔρωτα) of the supposed (νομιζομένης) mistress (δεσποίνης), at one time exhorting/pleading (παρακαλούσης) at another threatening (ἀπειλούσης), he did not even make mention (ὑπεμνήσθη) of the history. For we would see Joseph much better (κρείττονα) than the things told about Bellerophon, having chosen (ἑλόμενον) to be shut up (κατακλεισθῆναι) in prison rather than lose a chaste/sound mind; being able at any rate to make defence and plead his case against the woman who accused him, great-souledly he kept silent, having entrusted his affairs to God.
pass_b_english: Celsus tosses in besides “the hatred,” I suppose of Esau toward Jacob (Genesis 27:41), a man acknowledged in Scripture to be base. And without setting out clearly the story of Simeon and Levi, who avenged the outrage done to their sister when she was violated by the son of the king of Shechem (Genesis 34:1–31), he accuses them. He speaks of “brothers selling,” meaning the sons of Jacob, and “a brother being sold,” meaning Joseph, and “a father deceived,” meaning Jacob, since he suspected nothing of his sons when they showed him Joseph’s “many-coloured coat” (Genesis 37:32), but believed them and “mourned” for Joseph as lost while he was a slave in Egypt (Genesis 37:33–35).

But see how Celsus has gathered material from the history in hatred and not in love of truth. So, where the history seemed to him to contain grounds for accusation, he sets it out; but where it gives a notable display of chastity, when Joseph did not yield to the passion of the woman held to be his mistress, who now pleaded with him and now threatened him (Genesis 39:7–20), he did not so much as mention the history. For we would see that Joseph was far nobler than anything told of Bellerophon, since he chose to be shut up in prison rather than lose a chaste mind. Indeed, though he could have defended himself and argued his case against the woman who accused him, he kept a noble silence, entrusting his cause to God.

choices.choice: ὁμολογουμένου φαύλου: 'whom Scripture admits to be wicked' changed to 'acknowledged in Scripture to be base' (Scripture does not 'admit' anything; φαῦλος is 'base')
Restored the ὥστε link with 'So,' before 'where the history seemed to him'
Bellerophon comparison: 'Joseph is far better than the tales told of Bellerophon' (Joseph compared with tales) recast as 'far nobler than anything told of Bellerophon'; ἴδοιμεν ἄν as 'we would see'

Copy-text: staged source_4.json section 46 (Koetschau 4.46). Celsus’s catalogue items as reported: ‘the hatred’ (ἀπέχθεια), ‘brothers selling’, ‘a brother being sold’, ‘a father deceived’; their exact wording limits are not marked in this staged text. ‘A man acknowledged in Scripture to be base’ (ὁμολογουμένου φαύλου) refers to Esau (genitive in agreement with τοῦ Ἠσαῦ); compare Hebrews 12:16, not cited inline as it is not quoted. σφᾶς αἰτιᾶται read as ‘he accuses them’ (Simeon and Levi). ‘The son of the king of Shechem’: Shechem son of Hamor, ruler of the land (Genesis 34:2). The edition marks „τὸν ποικίλον χιτῶνα“ (Genesis 37:32 LXX τὸν χιτῶνα τὸν ποικίλον) and „ἐπένθει“ (Genesis 37:34 LXX ἐπένθει τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ) as Scripture; the closing mark of the second quotation is missing in the staged text, so only ‘mourned’ is put in quotation marks. ‘The woman held to be his mistress’ for τῆς νομιζομένης δεσποίνης: she was his mistress only in name, since he was wrongly enslaved. κρείττονα τῶν κατὰ τὸν Βελλεροφόντην ἱστορουμένων compares Joseph with what is told of Bellerophon, hence ‘far nobler than anything told of Bellerophon’. Bellerophon: the tale of Anteia’s false accusation is told in Homer, Iliad 6.155–170, but Origen refers to the tradition in general, so no classical citation is given inline. Joseph’s silence is inferred from Genesis 39:19–20, where no defence is recorded.
